cases.query: Do Uzbek nouns change form for masculine and feminine?

retrievedChunks.text:
Uzbek language > Grammar

Uzbek is generally agglutinative: grammatical information is often added through sequences of suffixes.

A common basic word order is subject-object-verb, although real Uzbek sentences can vary for emphasis and style.

Uzbek does not have grammatical gender comparable to languages such as Russian, French or German.

Uzbek language > Vocabulary

Uzbek has a Turkic grammatical core but contains many loanwords from Persian, Arabic, Russian and, more recently, international English-based vocabulary.

Uzbek language > Language family

Uzbek is a Turkic language. It belongs to the Karluk branch of the Turkic language family and is closely related historically and linguistically to Uyghur.

Uzbek language > Modern Latin alphabet features

Modern Uzbek Latin writing includes distinctive forms such as Oʻ/oʻ and Gʻ/gʻ, as well as the combinations Sh/sh, Ch/ch and Ng/ng.

cases.answer: No, Uzbek nouns do not change form for masculine and feminine because the language does not have grammatical gender.

cases.query: What abilities does a Bakhshi storyteller rely on most?

retrievedChunks.text:
Music, dance and oral traditions > Bakhshi art

Bakhshi are epic singers and storytellers who perform narrative poetry, often with musical accompaniment. The art depends heavily on memory, improvisation, oral transmission and apprenticeship.

Bakhshi art from Uzbekistan was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List in 2021.

Music, dance and oral traditions > Askiya

Askiya is an Uzbek verbal art based on witty dialogue and improvisation. Two or more performers exchange humorous remarks around a theme.

Successful performers need strong command of language, quick reasoning, observation and improvisation. UNESCO inscribed Askiya in 2014.

cases.query: Apart from schooling and factories, which areas of life did the Soviet state keep under tight control?

retrievedChunks.text:
Modern history and independence > Soviet modernization

Soviet rule expanded mass education, industrialization, transportation and urban development. It also introduced strong state control over politics, religion, culture, agriculture and publishing.

headingPath: History of the territory of present-day Uzbekistan
retrievedChunks.text:
History of the territory of present-day Uzbekistan > Soviet period

The Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic was created in 1924. Soviet rule transformed education, industry, agriculture, language policy and urban life. Cotton production expanded enormously, while large-scale irrigation contributed to the later environmental crisis of the Aral Sea.

Jadidism and modern reformers > Repression

Many major Jadid intellectuals were later accused of nationalism or anti-Soviet activity. A large part of the generation was killed or silenced during the Stalinist purges of the 1930s.

Modern history and independence > Stalinist repression

During the 1930s, many Uzbek and Central Asian intellectuals, including prominent writers and Jadids, were arrested, imprisoned or executed during Stalinist purges.

cases.answer: Apart from education and industry, the Soviet state maintained strict authority over politics, religion, culture, agriculture, and publishing. Additionally, the government tightly regulated language policy and directed large-scale agricultural projects, such as the massive expansion of cotton production.

Bibixonim jome masjidi Samarqandda 1399-1404 yillarda, Amir Temurning Hindiston yurishidan keyin qurilgan. U o'z davrida islom olamining eng katta masjidlaridan biri edi.

Timurid era > Samarkand under the Timurids

UNESCO identifies the 14th and 15th centuries as Samarkand's most significant period of development. Major monuments include Bibi-Khanum Mosque, Shah-i-Zinda, Gur-e Amir, Ulugh Beg's madrasa and Ulugh Beg's observatory.

Timurid era > Amir Temur

Amir Temur, known in many Western sources as Timur or Tamerlane, was born in 1336 near Kesh, the area of modern Shahrisabz. He rose to power in Transoxiana and established Samarkand as the main capital of his empire.

Timur's empire stretched across large parts of Central Asia, Iran, Afghanistan, the Caucasus and neighbouring regions. His campaigns were often destructive, while his court also concentrated craftsmen, scholars and architects in Samarkand.

Timur died in 1405. The Gur-e Amir mausoleum in Samarkand became his burial place and one of the best-known monuments associated with the dynasty.

Timurid era > Ulugh Beg

Ulugh Beg, a grandson of Timur, was a Timurid ruler and astronomer. He governed Samarkand and became famous for supporting mathematics and astronomy.

Ulugh Beg founded a major observatory in Samarkand in the 15th century. Astronomers working there produced highly accurate observations of stars and planetary motion for their time.

Ulugh Beg also built a madrasa on the Registan.

cases.answer: The Bibi-Khanum Mosque in Samarkand was built between 1399 and 1404, right after Amir Timur's campaign in India.

History of the territory of present-day Uzbekistan > Samanid period

The Samanids ruled much of Central Asia in the 9th and 10th centuries. Bukhara was one of the dynasty's major political and cultural centres and became famous for scholarship, literature and religious learning.

Historic cities and architecture > Bukhara

Bukhara has more than two thousand years of history and was a major centre on the Silk Roads.

UNESCO describes its historic centre as one of the best-preserved examples of a medieval Central Asian Islamic city.

The Ismail Samani Mausoleum is one of Bukhara's most famous early monuments and an outstanding example of 10th-century architecture.

Historic cities and architecture > Samarkand

Samarkand is one of Central Asia's oldest major cities. UNESCO describes it as a crossroads and melting pot of world cultures.

The ancient settlement of Afrasiab forms an archaeological part of the city's history. Major monuments include Registan Square, Bibi-Khanum Mosque, Shah-i-Zinda, Gur-e Amir and Ulugh Beg's Observatory.

headingPath: History of the territory of present-day Uzbekistan
retrievedChunks.text:
History of the territory of present-day Uzbekistan > Ancient and early medieval background

The territory of present-day Uzbekistan has long connected settled oasis civilizations, steppe peoples, and long-distance trade routes. Samarkand, Bukhara, Khiva, Termez and other cities developed at different times as political, commercial, religious and intellectual centres.

Samarkand grew from the ancient settlement known as Afrasiab. UNESCO describes the historic city as a major crossroads of cultures with more than two and a half millennia of history.

cases.answer: Bukhara was one of the major political, cultural, and scholarly centres of the Samanid dynasty during the 9th and 10th centuries.

cases.query: Which town is famous for blue-green glazed pottery?
cases.note: Distractor: Margilan (textiles).

retrievedChunks.text:
Crafts, textiles and material culture > Ceramics

Ceramic art is one of Uzbekistan's longstanding applied arts. Traditional pottery includes household vessels, jugs, storage containers, toys, architectural tiles and tandoor ovens.

Rishtan is especially famous for glazed ceramics and blue-green decorative traditions.

UNESCO inscribed Ceramic Arts in Uzbekistan on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2023.

Crafts, textiles and material culture > Atlas and adras

Atlas and adras are traditional ikat fabrics associated strongly with Central Asian textile culture. Margilan became one of the most famous centres of production in present-day Uzbekistan.

In 2017, UNESCO selected the Margilan Crafts Development Centre's work safeguarding atlas and adras techniques for its Register of Good Safeguarding Practices.

Historic cities and architecture > Khiva and Itchan Kala

Itchan Kala is the walled inner city of Khiva. UNESCO describes it as a fortified historic town with a history of more than two millennia.

The walled area contains madrasas, mosques, mausoleums, caravanserais, markets and traditional houses.

Historic cities and architecture > Bukhara

Bukhara has more than two thousand years of history and was a major centre on the Silk Roads.

UNESCO describes its historic centre as one of the best-preserved examples of a medieval Central Asian Islamic city.

The Ismail Samani Mausoleum is one of Bukhara's most famous early monuments and an outstanding example of 10th-century architecture.

cases.answer: Rishtan is especially famous for its glazed ceramics and blue-green decorative pottery traditions.

cases.query: Which embroidered textile was often part of a bride's dowry?

retrievedChunks.text:
Crafts, textiles and material culture > Suzani

Suzani is a traditional embroidered textile associated with settled communities in Central Asia, especially areas of present-day Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.

Historically, large suzanis were used to decorate interiors and were often part of a bride's dowry.

Crafts, textiles and material culture > Atlas and adras

Atlas and adras are traditional ikat fabrics associated strongly with Central Asian textile culture. Margilan became one of the most famous centres of production in present-day Uzbekistan.

In 2017, UNESCO selected the Margilan Crafts Development Centre's work safeguarding atlas and adras techniques for its Register of Good Safeguarding Practices.

Modern history and independence > Cotton and the Aral Sea

Uzbekistan became one of the Soviet Union's major cotton-producing regions. Extensive irrigation projects diverted water from the Amu Darya and Syr Darya systems.

The reduction of water reaching the Aral Sea contributed to one of the world's major environmental disasters.

Culture and social life > Palov

Palov is one of the best-known dishes of Uzbekistan. It is commonly prepared with rice, meat, vegetables, oil or fat, and spices, although recipes vary by region and family.

UNESCO notes that palov is served both as an everyday meal and at important social occasions, including weddings, celebrations, acts of hospitality and commemorative gatherings.

cases.answer: Suzani is a traditional embroidered textile that was historically used to decorate interiors and was often included as part of a bride's dowry.
